newsitem.title: USA: Two Mexican governors linked to drug trade -report.
newsitem.headline: Two Mexican governors linked to drug trade -report.

text.p: Two Mexican state governors have collaborated with drug trafficking rings but enjoy a political immunity that has frustrated investigators in both Mexico and the United States, the New York Times reported on Sunday.

The newspaper, citing U.S. officials and intelligence sources, said the governor of the border state of Sonora, Manilo Fabio Beltrones, had helped create a haven for smugglers who ship vast quantities of drugs into the United States.

Beltrones took part in meetings in which leading traffickers paid high-level politicians, including Raul Salinas, the brother of Mexico's former president, with suitcases full of cash for protecting their operations, the officials told the paper.

The evidence against Beltrones, whose state borders Arizona, was so strong that the United States named him in a confidential report to the transition team of President Ernesto Zedillo listing Mexican officials suspected of corruption, the New York Times said.
The governor of Morelos state, Jorge Carrillo Olea, was also on the U.S. blacklist because of reported links with major drug dealers, the paper said.
Both governors have denied the allegations.
The Times said officials on both sides of the border were frustrated by the tacit immunity enjoyed by the governors.

Mexico suddenly arrested its top drug warrior last week on charges he took money from the country's most powerful cocaine lord. The dismissal of the top drug fighter, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, embarrassed both the U.S. and the Mexican governments.
Despite recent disclosures of corruption, the Clinton administration is planning to certify later this month that Mexico is cooperating with anti-drug efforts, the Times said.
Senior officials told the paper the decision reflects a belief that Mexico's leadership is doing all it can against staggering odds.

Law enforcement officials feel the Clinton administration considers the narcotics war less important than fostering commerce with Mexico, the United States' third largest trade partner, the Times said.
